title: The battle inside
hookLine: how a book set on a battlefield became Gandhi's guide to nonviolence, and Tilak's call to act
carry: anasakti: act fully, don't cling to the fruit

cards: London, the late eighteen-eighties. A young law student from Gujarat meets two brothers who ask him to read the Gita with them. He's embarrassed: he's never read it, not in Sanskrit, not in Gujarati.
So he meets it first in English, in Edwin Arnold's poem The Song Celestial. His name is Mohandas Gandhi.
Years later, in South Africa, he copies verses onto slips of paper and learns them by heart while he gets ready each morning, and the Gita becomes, as he put it, his dictionary of daily reference.

teach.b: But the Gita is set on a battlefield, and Krishna is telling Arjuna to fight. How does a man of nonviolence live by it? Gandhi read the battle as the war inside every person, between what's better and worse in us.
And he took from the Gita one teaching above all: act fully, and let go of the fruit.
In nineteen twenty-nine he finished a Gujarati translation and called it Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment.

teach.h: TILAK: ACTION, FROM A JAIL CELL.
teach.b: Hindus also call this nishkama karma, action without craving: do what's right completely, without clinging to how it turns out. It's chapter two, verse forty-seven: your right is to the action, not its fruit.
Now Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Jailed by the British in Mandalay, in Burma, he wrote a long Marathi commentary, the Gita Rahasya, published in nineteen fifteen.
His reading: the Gita's heart is karma yoga, energetic action in the world, and duty can include resisting wrong by force.
Same book, same verse about the fruit, and the two men disagreed sharply. That argument is still alive. But what both men kept is the teaching itself.
Work for what's right with everything you have, and don't let the result own you.
A student before an exam, a volunteer in the temple kitchen, someone fighting for a cause that may not win in their lifetime: do the work, offer the fruit.

how: Many Hindus speak of nishkama karma, action without craving for the result, and try to work this way, often offering the work to God; Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga and Tilak's Gita Rahasya are still widely read in India.

games.q: you're Gandhi. a book you love has God telling a warrior to fight, and you're committed to nonviolence. what do you take from it?
o: throw it out: it's a war book.
read the battle as the war inside, and keep its core: act fully, let go of the fruit.
games.why: Anasakti Yoga, 1929. Tilak, reading the same book, argued duty can include force.

practice: Think of one thing you're working toward that you can't fully control: a grade, a game, someone's answer. If you pray, offer it, as many Hindus do: the work is mine, the fruit is yours.
If you don't, say to yourself: I'll do my part fully, and let the result go. Then picture tomorrow's piece of it, done wholeheartedly, with open hands.
